entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
Les Fleurs du Mal is a foundational volume of French poetry by Charles Baudelaire, created circa 1840. This collection of poems explores the darker aspects of human nature and the urban experience, influencing generations of poets and thinkers.

Baudelaire's work was initially published in serial form in L'Incroyable, a Parisian literary magazine, before being compiled into book form in 1857. The title "Les Fleurs du Mal" translates to "The Flowers of Evil," and reflects the collection's themes of decay, corruption, and the struggle for beauty in a chaotic world.

Les Fleurs du Mal had a profound impact on modern French literature and culture, shaping the development of Symbolism and influencing artists such as Edgar Degas and Claude Monet. The book's success also helped establish Baudelaire as one of France's greatest poets and cemented his reputation as a leading figure in the Parisian literary salons.

Today, Les Fleurs du Mal remains a vital work of literature, widely studied and translated around the world. Its exploration of the human condition continues to resonate with readers and inspire new generations of writers and artists.

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "Les Fleurs du mal ('The Flowers of Evil') is a collection of poems by the French poet Charles Baudelaire (1821–1867), first published in Paris on 25 June 1857 by the publisher Poulet-Malassis, immediately condemned as obscene by a French court (Baudelaire, his publisher, and his printer were convicted; six poems were ordered suppressed; the conviction was overturned only in 1949), and recognised in the 20th century as the most important collection of French poetry of the 19th century and a founding document of literary Modernism. The first edition contained 100 poems; the second edition (1861, after the suppression of six poems) contained 126 poems; a posthumous third edition (1868) added 25 more, for a total of 151.

Les Fleurs du mal is organised into six sections: 'Spleen et Idéal' (the largest, containing the great lyric poems of beauty, melancholy, and the tension between spiritual aspiration and sensual experience), 'Tableaux Parisiens' (urban poems of Paris, the anonymous modern city), 'Le Vin', 'Fleurs du Mal', 'Révolte', and 'La Mort' (death as the final escape). The collection's central subject is the tension between spleen (ennui, acedia, spiritual deadness) and idéal (spiritual aspiration, beauty, transcendence) — a tension that Baudelaire finds in the most repulsive subjects (decay, prostitution, the city's underworld, death) as well as the most beautiful. The famous opening poem, 'Au Lecteur' ('To the Reader'), addresses the reader directly as a fellow sinner: 'Hypocrite lecteur, — mon semblable, — mon frère!' ('Hypocrite reader — my likeness — my brother!')

Baudelaire's innovations — the concept of 'correspondances' (synesthetic connections between senses, the idea that perfumes, colours, and sounds correspond to one another and to spiritual states), the idea of the poet as an alienated figure ('spleen'), the urban flaneur, the erotic poem as a form of spiritual investigation — inaugurated the Symbolist movement (Verlaine, Rimbaud, Mallarmé) and, through Symbolism, Modernism.
